summary: Provides additional procedures for handling SIP re-INVITE and target-refresh requests, fixing issues found with the original text of RFC 3261, including when a user agent server should respond with success. It updates RFC 3261 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Changing a call already in progress, like adding video, was described unclearly. This clears it up so phones agree.

questions: when to accept or reject a re-invite
how to handle session changes during a call
subtitle: Clarifies how to modify a call already in progress and refresh contact addresses.

tldr.problem: The original SIP specification left several situations unclear, particularly when a server should accept or reject requests that modify an ongoing call, and how contact address changes should be handled.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines when to respond with success versus error, how to handle partially executed changes, and rules for refreshing the remote contact address even during long-lived transactions.
tldr.outcome: SIP implementations can now reliably modify ongoing calls and handle address changes without both endpoints losing synchronization.

today: RFC 6141 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3261. It clarifies the procedures for handling re-INVITE and target-refresh requests and is widely implemented in SIP endpoints and servers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A re-INVITE is an INVITE request sent within an existing SIP dialog to modify the call. It can change what media streams are active (adding or removing video, for example), what codec is used, or the contact address where the remote party should reach you.

The original SIP specification left several situations unclear, particularly around when a server should accept or reject a re-INVITE and what happens when the server has already started executing some changes before deciding to reject others. This RFC addresses those issues and also clarifies how the contact addresses that endpoints use to reach each other should be refreshed during the call.
sections.eli5: When you want to change a call that is happening, you send a special message. This says when to say yes or no to that request.

sections.title: Session Changes and Error Responses
sections.content:
A fundamental principle: if a server has already started executing changes requested in a re-INVITE (for example, if it has sent or received media using new parameters), it MUST NOT send an error response to reject those changes. Instead, it sends a success response.

The reason is that an error response would signal to the client: 'nothing changed.' But if the server has already changed things, this is a lie. The client would then have no way to know the server's state is different. Instead, the server should send a successful response showing which changes it is keeping and which it is reverting.

A server can immediately reject a re-INVITE only if it has not yet executed any of the requested changes. In all other cases, it should send a 2xx response and use other transactions (such as UPDATE) to revert any unwanted changes before that 2xx response.
sections.eli5: If you already used what someone asked for, you can't say no to the request. You have to say yes and then explain which parts you kept.

sections.title: Target Refresh: Updating Contact Addresses
sections.content:
During a dialog, each endpoint keeps track of the contact address where it can reach the other endpoint. When an endpoint moves to a new network and gets a new IP address, it must refresh this contact address.

A re-INVITE can carry a new contact address. The RFC clarifies when each endpoint should consider a contact refresh complete. If the server sends a reliable response (provisional or final success), the client updates its record. If the server generates an error response, the client does NOT update its record. However, if the server receives an in-dialog request on the new address, it knows the client has recorded the new address.

The rules also address race conditions: if both endpoints are trying to change the contact at the same time, each should prefer to use a request (rather than a response) to communicate its new address, so that both endpoints agree on the order of updates.
sections.eli5: When you move and get a new phone number, you need to tell the other person. This explains when they know you've successfully told them and when messages might cross.

sections.title: The Offer/Answer Exchange
sections.content:
Every re-INVITE involves an exchange of session descriptions (SDP) between the two endpoints. One endpoint makes an offer (proposing changes), the other makes an answer (accepting, rejecting, or modifying them).

A single re-INVITE transaction can be long-lived and involve multiple offer/answer exchanges. For example, one endpoint might send an offer in the re-INVITE, the other might respond with an answer in a provisional response (indicating 'I understand your offer but need user input'). Meanwhile, an UPDATE request might carry another offer/answer between those two messages.

The RFC clarifies that changes to the session parameters are considered executed once an offer/answer exchange completes successfully, or when media actually starts flowing with new parameters. Simply exchanging SDP with preconditions does not execute changes; the changes are only executed when those preconditions are met or when the endpoint decides to use the new parameters.
sections.eli5: Think of it like a negotiation: you suggest something, the other person responds, maybe you negotiate more. Once you both agree and start doing it, the change is real.

sections.title: Handling Glare and Race Conditions
sections.content:
A glare condition occurs when both endpoints send offers at the same time, creating ambiguity about which should take precedence. The original SIP specification provided rules to avoid most glare situations, and when they still occur, the specification says to retry.

This RFC adds rules for cases the original specification did not cover, such as when one endpoint sends an UPDATE request carrying an offer while the other endpoint sends a non-2xx response to a re-INVITE. Additionally, if a UAC receives an error response to a re-INVITE that appears to undo already-executed changes, the RFC recommends sending a new re-INVITE to synchronize both endpoints' understanding of the session state.

Special attention is given to situations where an endpoint moves to a new network address during an ongoing re-INVITE transaction. In these cases, the endpoint might not receive the response to the re-INVITE. The RFC provides guidance so that both endpoints can recover gracefully without terminating the dialog.
sections.eli5: If you both talk at the same time, the rules say how to sort it out so you both agree on what happened.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
This RFC does not introduce new security issues; it simply clarifies existing SIP procedures. However, it reinforces that re-INVITEs and UPDATE requests should be protected with the same security mechanism as the original INVITE that created the dialog.

For example, if the initial INVITE was encrypted end-to-end, so should subsequent re-INVITEs and UPDATEs be. This ensures that the security level of the call does not degrade during modifications.
sections.eli5: Keep your call changes as safe as you kept the original call.
